mathgap.title: Sequential Transfer Application
mathgap.principle: When a statement says 'X gives N items to Y', immediately subtract N from X's current count and add N to Y's count, updating both counts for subsequent statements.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a transfer statement of the form 'X gives N items to Y' appears.
mathgap.example: Assuming X's count remains unchanged after giving N items to Y, leading to an incorrect total.

mathgap.title: Signed Interpretation of "has K more than"
mathgap.principle: Interpret 'A has K more than B' as the signed equation A − B = K (or A = B + K), preserving the order of A and B, regardless of the sign of K.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a comparative statement with a numeric difference appears.
mathgap.example: Treating 'A has K more than B' as B = A + K, swapping the direction.

mathgap.title: Signed Equality for Difference Statements
mathgap.principle: For statements like 'The number of items that A has more than B is equal to the difference between the number of items that C and D have', interpret as (A − B) = (C − D), preserving the order on each side.
mathgap.example: Treating the equality as |A − B| = |C − D|, ignoring sign.

mathgap.title: Current‑Count Constraint for "has N"
mathgap.principle: A statement 'A has N items' fixes A's count at that point in the narrative, after any earlier transfers or updates.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a direct count statement appears.
mathgap.example: Assuming the count is an immutable initial value and not updating it after later transfers.

mathgap.title: Iterative Substitution and Propagation
mathgap.principle: Whenever a variable's value becomes known, substitute it into all pending equations and simplify, propagating constraints throughout the system.
mathgap.when_to_apply: After solving any variable, update all other equations that involve it.
mathgap.example: Leaving a known variable unchanged in later equations, missing simplifications.

mathgap.title: Consistency Check After Solving
mathgap.principle: After assigning values to all variables, verify each original statement—including transfers, direct counts, and difference equalities—to ensure the solution satisfies all constraints.
mathgap.when_to_apply: At the end of solving, before outputting the answer.
mathgap.example: Accepting a solution that violates a previously stated equality.

mathgap.title: Chronological Evaluation of Comparative Statements
mathgap.principle: Interpret comparative statements using the counts as they exist at that point in the narrative, after any earlier transfers or updates, not using initial counts.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When processing statements in order, especially those that compare variables whose values may have changed.
mathgap.example: Using a person's initial count for a later comparison after they have given away items.

mathgap.title: Query‑Focused Subsystem Extraction
mathgap.principle: Identify the subset of equations and statements that involve the queried person directly or through other variables, and solve only that subsystem to reduce unnecessary complexity.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When the problem contains many irrelevant statements.
mathgap.example: Attempting to solve the entire system of equations, including unrelated variables, leading to confusion.

mathgap.title: Equal Redistribution Handling
mathgap.principle: When a statement says 'X and Y redistribute their items to ensure each has an equal amount', pool their current counts and assign each half of the total.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a redistribution statement between two persons appears.
mathgap.example: Leaving the original counts unchanged after a redistribution, missing the equal split.

mathgap.title: Equal Split Handling
mathgap.principle: When a statement says 'X splits all the items they own equally among Y and Z', set X's count to zero and add half of X's previous count to each of Y and Z (assuming the total is divisible by two).
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a split operation where one person distributes all their items equally to multiple recipients appears.
mathgap.example: Treating the split as a simple transfer of the whole amount to one recipient, or forgetting to zero out the splitter's count.

mathgap.description: Swapped direction in "has K more than" statements
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model may focus on the phrase "more than" and mistakenly place the difference on the wrong side of the equation.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Always map the statement to A − B = K, preserving the order of A and B as they appear.

mathgap.why_it_happens: The model assumes "difference" means magnitude, ignoring the signed nature required by the puzzle.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Interpret "difference between C and D" as the signed expression (C − D), preserving order.

mathgap.description: Ignoring the chronological order of transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model may treat all statements as simultaneous constraints rather than a sequence of events.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Process statements sequentially, updating counts after each transfer before evaluating later statements.

mathgap.description: Treating "has N" as an initial count regardless of position
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model assumes a "has N" clause defines a fixed value that never changes.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Interpret "has N" as fixing the count at that point in the narrative, after any earlier updates.

mathgap.description: Assuming all "more than" differences must be positive
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model expects natural‑language "more than" to indicate a positive difference.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Treat "has more than" as a signed equation without imposing positivity; the sign may be negative if the narrative forces it.
